title: The DNA
eyebrow: Three estimates, the wall they hit, and one chromosome that goes through it
dek: MyHeritage v2.5 for David and both his parents, read against 1,129 named people and four hundred years of parish registers — and, since 14 September 2026, a Y-DNA haplogroup for the male line.
lead: Three people in this family have taken the same test, and the results were updated to **MyHeritage's v2.5 model** this month. Set side by side they do something the registers cannot: they say what is in the body now, rather than what a clerk wrote down. They also do something the registers never would — **they disagree with each other, and with arithmetic.** A child is exactly half of each parent. The percentages are not. That is not an error in the test and it is not a surprise in the family; it is what these models do, and this page is mostly about learning to read them honestly. **An ethnicity estimate is not a document.** It is a statistical fit of one person's genome against reference panels of living people, expressed to one decimal place because the software can, not because the world is that precise. This archive grades every claim **doc**, **inf** or **lore**. These numbers get a fourth grade of their own — **dna** — and it ranks below *doc*, because a register entry names a person and an estimate names a probability. **Since 14 September 2026 there is a fourth reading on this page, and it is a different kind of thing.** A **Y-DNA haplogroup** is not a statistical fit against reference panels — it is a mutation, present or absent, on the one chromosome that passes father to son intact. It is the only evidence in this archive that runs straight up the male line, and it is the only one that does not agree with the paper. It is at the Y chromosome below.

midpoint.heading: Half of each, and yet not
midpoint.lead:
If these numbers behaved like inheritance, David's column would be the average of his parents'. Here is what happens when you actually take the midpoint.

**The total drift is 42.4 percentage points.** Every row moves. The largest movements are all in one direction: **Balkan is 13 points higher than it should be**, and the three British-Isles groups together are **ten points lower** — 23.3 expected, 13.4 measured.
midpoint.close:
Three rows land dead on the midpoint — **Danish**, **South Italian** and, to a tenth of a point, **Breton**. Two of Ivan's disappear entirely: his **4.0% Baltic** and, from Cheryl, **Sardinian** and **Swedish**, all of which fall under the reporting floor once halved.

The reason is that these models do not blend, they **assign**. A stretch of chromosome is given to whichever reference population fits it best, and a person of mixed descent has long stretches that could plausibly go either way. Where the two sides of a family are far apart genetically — a Kvarner Croat and a woman of the Low Countries and the British Isles — the more sharply defined population tends to win the contested segments. **Balkan is a tighter cluster than 'English'**, which is itself a blend of everything that ever landed there. So Balkan takes segments that a strict accounting would have split, and the British share shrinks.

*Germanic goes the other way* — **8.6% in David against a 2.6% midpoint**, higher than either parent's contribution allows. That is the same effect running in reverse: Germanic sits geographically between his mother's Dutch and his father's East European, and it collects the segments that neither cluster claims outright.

meet.heading: Where the DNA and the registers meet
meet.text:
One sub-cluster appears in **both** David and his father, and it is the only one David inherits: **«Croatia (Lika-Senj and Primorje-Gorski Kotar)»**.

Those are two named Croatian counties, and this archive can tell you exactly who lived in them.

**Primorje-Gorski Kotar** holds **Crikvenica**, where Josip Defranceschi went from Gračišće and where the family kept a house; and **Klenovica**, house 22, where Anton Rudolf was born in 1890. **Lika-Senj** holds **Senj**, where Ivan Defranceski (1925–1995) ended up. Those are **generations 4, 5 and 6** of the direct line — David's great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather and grandfather.

Ivan's second additional group says it again in different words: **«Croatia (Primorje-Gorski Kotar) and Southeastern Austria»** — the Kvarner littoral and the Habsburg hinterland behind it, which is precisely the administrative world these registers were kept in. His third, **«Czechia, Poland, Germany, Hungary and Austria»**, is the empire itself.

**This is the closest thing to a confirmation this archive has ever had from outside its own paper.** A genetic cluster built from strangers' saliva names the same two counties that a Croatian parish clerk was writing into a book in 1890. Neither knew about the other.

horizon.heading: The horizon, and why Carnia is invisible
horizon.lead:
Now the part that matters more than any percentage. **Ivan's estimate contains no Italian at all.** Not North Italian, not South Italian, not a fraction.

This archive's founding story is that the name came **out of Carnia** — the Val Degano in Friuli — and reached Istria by about **1679**. If that is true, why is there no Italian in the father's DNA?

Because **there was never going to be.** Autosomal DNA halves every generation, and it halves fast:
horizon.close:
The reporting floor on these estimates is around **1%**. Read the table again with that in mind: **everything older than Giovanni Battista, born 1787, is beneath the floor** — and that is on the direct male line, which is the *slowest*-diluting path a surname takes.

So the Carnian origin is not contradicted by the DNA. **It is simply out of range.** An ancestor of 1679 contributes about **one part in a thousand** of a living descendant's genome, twenty times less than the test can see. The Omiš chart's fourteenth-century man contributes a number with four zeros after the decimal point.

This is the single most useful thing on this page. **The paper reaches back to 1318. The DNA reaches back about six generations, to roughly 1790.** They are not two views of the same distance. Where they overlap — Kvarner, generations 4 to 6 — they agree exactly. Beyond that overlap, the DNA has nothing to say, and **an absence of Italian is not evidence against Carnia**. It is evidence that the test works as designed.

groups.heading: The genetic groups are a map of last century, not the middle ages
groups.text:
The coloured continents are deep ancestry. The **genetic groups** listed beneath them are something else entirely — clusters of *living* testers who share recent ancestry in one place. They are a record of **where a family was two or three generations ago**, and they are blunt about it.

David carries four: **South Africa #2, South Africa and Zimbabwe, South Africa #3, South Africa (Gauteng and Free State)** — and **England**. His father carries none of them. Every one comes through his mother, whose own list reads **South Africa, South Africa and Zimbabwe**, and **Argentina (Corrientes and Buenos Aires)**.

That is the maternal family's twentieth century written in genetic shorthand: the **Low Countries and the British Isles by descent, southern Africa by residence** — Gauteng and the Free State named outright — with a strand running to the Argentine littoral. The direct line's own migration is in the same list from the other side: David was born in **Johannesburg**, and his father came to it from **Senj**.

These groups do not date anything and they do not name anybody. What they do is tell you **where to write next** — and on the maternal side this archive has written almost nothing.

**One of those groups now has a person behind it.** Cheryl's father — **Nuno Fernando, called Larry** — was born in South Africa, and **his father came from Argentina** while **his mother came from England**. That is a documentary explanation for two things the estimate had only guessed at: the **Argentina (Corrientes and Buenos Aires)** cluster, and a share of the English. **A genetic group is a question; this is the first time a family document has answered one.**

greek.heading: Ten per cent Greek and Albanian
greek.text: Ivan's estimate carries **10.3% Greek and Albanian**, a tenth of him, and it survives into David at **2.5%**. In the eastern Adriatic this is not exotic. It is partly the deep Balkan substrate that every population on that coast shares, and partly something more specific: for four centuries the Venetian *Stato da Màr* moved Greek and Albanian people up and down this sea — the **Arbanasi** settled outside Zadar in the 1720s, Greek communities held churches in Venice, Trieste and the Dalmatian ports, and Venetian galleys carried crews from every shore they touched. This archive already has **a family out of Crete at Seget**. That is a *different* family and no connection is claimed — but it is worth saying that a Greek-and-Albanian tenth in a Kvarner man is exactly what four hundred years of Venetian sea traffic would leave behind, and the registers on At sea are full of the ships that did it.

terms.heading: What this counts as, in this archive's terms
rows: A statistical fit against reference panels of living people. It describes a probability, not a person. It cannot name anybody, cannot date anything, and goes blind past about six generations.
Whether a broad regional origin is plausible within the last two centuries — and, through genetic groups, roughly where a family lived two or three generations back.
Any individual link. No percentage on this page joins one named person to another, and none of the 1,129 people in this archive was put there by a test.
**An absence in an estimate is not a denial in a register.** Carnia is invisible here because it is 0.098% of a genome, not because it did not happen.
And the exception to all of it

**A Y haplogroup is not an estimate and none of the four limits above apply to it.** It is a single inherited marker, it does not dilute, and it reaches as far back as the male line itself. What it cannot do is the opposite of what the percentages cannot do: it can say a lineage is unexpected, but it **cannot name a generation, cannot date one, and cannot identify an event**. See the Y chromosome.

privacy: Two of the three people on this page are **living**. This archive's rule for living people is name only — no dates, no places of residence, no photographs — and that rule is kept here: neither parent is dated or placed. An ethnicity estimate is more than a name, and it is published because **David asked for it to be**. If either would rather it were not, it comes down on request.
source: MyHeritage DNA, Ethnicity Estimate **v2.5**, read 10 September 2026 from David's own account. Percentages as displayed. The genetic-groups confidence slider affects only which sub-clusters are listed, not the ethnicity percentages, so the three columns are directly comparable. Generation arithmetic is the plain halving 1/2ⁿ and takes no account of recombination luck, which in a single case can move a small share by a factor of two either way.

notable.heading: Notable individuals, and the trap in the number
notable.lead:
The same test offers a list of **notable individuals** whose ancient DNA has been sequenced, ranked by a **Genetic Fit** score. The scale runs the wrong way round: **lower is closer.** Under 1.0 is «very close», 1.0–3.0 «close», 3.0–5.0 «moderate», above 5.0 «distant».

The temptation is obvious. **King Béla III of Hungary, Croatia and Dalmatia** sits at the top of David's list at **2.196**, the best score anyone in this family has, and it is very easy to read that as a line of descent from a medieval king.

It is not one, and the three lists prove it themselves.

Lutheran bishop of Lund, 1605–1679, whose preserved body still lies in the cathedral

impossible.heading: A son cannot out-descend his parents
impossible.text:
Eight of these people appear on all three lists. **On five of the eight, David scores closer than his father *and* his mother.**

That is not a curiosity, it is a proof. Every scrap of David's DNA came from one of those two people. If the score measured *descent*, being nearer to Béla III than either parent would be arithmetically impossible — you cannot inherit more of a man than your parents had to give.

The clearest case is **Peder Winstrup**, a bishop of Lund who died in 1679. Ivan scores **4.046**, Cheryl Anne **4.176** — both «moderate». David scores **2.845**, which is a whole band better, «close», and **1.201 nearer than the best either parent manages.**

What the score actually measures is stated plainly in the test's own note: *how well a combination of ancient reference populations aligns with your genetics*. It compares **profiles**, not pedigrees. A Kvarner Croat sits at one point on that map; a woman of the Low Countries, the British Isles and a little Scandinavia sits at another; and their son sits **between them** — which is, as it happens, roughly where a seventeenth-century Scanian bishop, a Saxon architect and a medieval Hungarian king all sit too.

**The blend is the whole effect.** David is not closer to these people than his parents are. He is closer to the *middle*, and they lived in the middle.

behaves.heading: And yet it is not noise
behaves.text:
If the score were meaningless, the two parents' lists would be interchangeable. They are not, and the differences fall exactly where descent says they should.

**Philip Calvert**, an English colonial governor of Maryland, appears on **David's list and his mother's — and not on his father's.** She is the parent with 13.7% English, 14.7% Irish and 18.2% Scottish and Welsh. **Jean-Paul Marat** appears on **hers alone**; she is the parent with 5.1% French.

Running the other way, the two **Rurikid princes** — Gleb Svyatoslavich and Izyaslav Ingvarevich, of the house that ruled Kyiv and Novgorod — appear on **David's list and his father's, and not on his mother's**. He is the parent with 20.8% East European and 4.0% Baltic. **King Ladislaus I** appears on his father's alone.

So the method is doing something real at the level of **regions**. It is only when it is read as a family tree that it collapses.

gap.heading: Nobody has sequenced a medieval Istrian
gap.text:
Read the fourteen names again and notice what is not there. **There is no Italian on any of the three lists. No Croatian. No Venetian, no Istrian, no Friulian, nobody from Carnia or Vodnjan or Senj.**

The list is Hungarian and Transylvanian nobility, princes of the Rus', a Saxon architect, a Scanian bishop, a German composer, a Bronze Age battlefield in Mecklenburg, an English colonist and a French revolutionary.

That is not a statement about this family. **It is a statement about which graves have been opened and paid for.** Ancient-DNA projects have concentrated on Hungarian royal tombs, Rurikid burials, and a handful of famous individuals; the medieval dead of the eastern Adriatic have largely not been sequenced. A list of notable individuals is a **map of published research**, and this family's own coast is a blank on it.

It is the same rule as the rest of this page, in a new dress: **an absence in the data is a fact about the data.**

resonance.heading: Three of them ruled this coast
resonance.text: One thing is worth keeping, stated for what it is — **a resonance, not a relationship.** The name at the top of David's list, **Béla III**, was king of *Hungary, Croatia and Dalmatia*. **Ladislaus I**, on his father's list, is the king who took Croatia in **1091** and founded the bishopric of Zagreb. And **John Corvinus**, on all three lists, was **Ban of Croatia and Dalmatia** at the end of the fifteenth century. Three of the fourteen held the crown or the office that governed the shore this family lived on. **Senj**, where Ivan Defranceski ended up, was a **royal free city of that kingdom**; the Vinodol coast below it was held from the same crown. That is not descent. It is something quieter and, for an archive that keeps a sovereignty chart, more interesting: the population of the Carpathian basin and the Croatian littoral has been one interbreeding world for a thousand years, and a genetic profile from it will land near the people who ruled it — **because they came out of it too.**

notable.source: MyHeritage DNA, Ancient Origins → Notable Individuals, read 10 September 2026 for all three kits. Scores as displayed, to three decimals. The Genetic Fit scale and its bands are the test's own. Lists are the top eleven shown for each person and are not exhaustive; a name absent from one list may simply fall below its eleventh place.

ydna.heading: The Y chromosome, and the one thing it does not confirm
ydna.lead:
On 14 September 2026 MyHeritage released a **Y-DNA haplogroup** for David and for his father. It is the only reading on this page that is not an estimate. An ethnicity percentage is a statistical fit; a haplogroup is a mutation, present or absent, and it is carried on the one chromosome that passes from father to son without recombining with anything.

That makes it the single piece of evidence in this archive that runs **straight up the male line** — Ivan, his father, his father's father, and back through every De Franceschi who ever signed a register, without a mother anywhere in it.

Both men return the same haplogroup. It is **L-M27**.

And L-M27 is not a European lineage.

call.heading: What the two kits say
call.note: Father and son agree, which is what a paternal line is supposed to do — the reading is at least **internally consistent**, and nothing here casts any doubt on the link between these two men.

freq.heading: Where L-M27 lives
freq.lead: The same test publishes how often the haplogroup turns up among its own testers, by the country each tester names as the origin of their direct paternal line. This is the whole of the top of that table, and then the two rows that matter to this family.
freq.close:
**Italy is on the list.** Five men out of six thousand, but they are there, and that matters more than the headline does: this lineage is **rare** on the Adriatic, not **impossible** on it. **Croatia is not on the list at all** — which means no Croatian tester in the panel has reported it, not that no Croatian carries it.

The archive states the rarity and refuses the leap. *Rare* is a probability. *Impossible* would be a claim, and nothing here supports one.

both.heading: How both readings can be true at once
both.text: Set the Y beside the autosomes and they appear to contradict each other flatly. **The autosomes say Kvarner.** Ivan's estimate is **100% European** — Balkan 64.9%, East European 20.8%, Greek and Albanian 10.3%, Baltic 4.0% — and his strongest sub-cluster is **«Croatia (Lika-Senj and Primorje-Gorski Kotar)»**, which is Senj and the coast under it. There is **no South Asian component and no Middle Eastern component**, at any confidence setting. David's estimate is the same story diluted by his mother: European, to the last decimal place. **The Y says something else entirely.** There is no contradiction, and the reason is arithmetic. **Autosomal ancestry halves every generation.** A single foreign ancestor contributes a quarter to a grandchild, a sixteenth four generations down, and less than **1%** — the reporting floor on these estimates — after about **seven generations**. He becomes invisible. **The Y chromosome does not halve.** It passes whole, unchanged but for the occasional mutation, for as long as the line produces sons. So one man, far enough back, leaves **a Y chromosome and no ethnicity at all**. That is precisely the pattern on this page. If an L-M27 man entered this paternal line more than roughly eight generations above Ivan — before about **1750**, which is where these registers are still thin — the estimates would look exactly as they look. This archive's own rule said the estimates go blind past about six generations. **The Y is the one reading here that does not go blind.** It is also, for the first time, a reading from outside the paper that does not agree with it.

limits.heading: What this is not, and it is important
limits.text:
**This is not a Y-DNA test.** MyHeritage reads the haplogroup off the *same autosomal microarray chip* that produced the ethnicity percentages. Those chips carry a limited and uneven scatter of Y markers. That is enough to place a man on a major branch of the tree; it is **not** enough to place him on a twig, and it is not the same instrument as a dedicated Y test.

**Two kits agreeing is not two tests agreeing.** David and his father return the same call, and if both kits ran on the same chip a systematic error would produce exactly that agreement. This archive does not know which platform each kit used, and says so rather than assuming.

**Nothing here identifies a generation.** A haplogroup is a fact about a lineage, not an event with a date. This page does **not** claim a break in the male line at any point, does not name one, and has no basis to. What it reports is a marker and an inconsistency with expectation — and the honest position is that the inconsistency has more than one explanation, including a rare-but-real European L-M27 of the kind those five Italians carry.

**The part that would say *when* is behind a paywall.** The Time Tree — the branch structure and the dates on it — is locked, and unlocks only with a **Big Y-700** from FamilyTreeDNA.
limits.grade: This section is graded **disputed**: the observation is documented, the reading of it is not settled, and the instrument is not the right one for the question.

ancient.heading: Two men in a cave in Armenia
ancient.text:
The test matches the lineage against published ancient genomes, and for L-M27 it returns two — both from the same place, and it is a place worth naming.

**Areni 44** (4330–4056 BCE) and **Areni 46** (4230–4000 BCE), both male, both from **Areni, Armenia**, both catalogued as *Copper Age Caucasian*. Areni 44 carries **Y-DNA L-M27** and **mtDNA H2a1**; Areni 46 carries **L-FTA37789** and **K1a8***. They are samples **I1634** and **I1632**, published in **Lazaridis et al. 2016** and carried forward into the **Allen Ancient Genome Diversity Project** and **Akbari et al. 2026**.

Areni-1 is the cave that produced the oldest known leather shoe and the oldest known winemaking installation in the world. The shared paternal ancestor is placed at about **6500 BCE**.

That is eight and a half thousand years ago and it says **nothing whatever about this family**. It is deep prehistory, and it belongs on this page as what it is — the furthest back a single unbroken thread of this line can currently be followed, and a genuinely published pair of skeletons at the end of it.

sayyid.heading: And one name that is not evidence
sayyid.text:
The same feature offers a **notable connection**: **Sayyid Ajall Shams al-Din Omar al-Bukhari** (1211–1279), the first provincial governor of Yunnan, whose descendants include the Ming admiral **Zheng He**, and whose male-line descendants were shown to carry **L1a-M76** in a 2013 study arguing a southern Persian origin for the family.

The test rates the connection **rare — 1 in 782**. The shared paternal ancestor is placed at **13,000 BCE**.

Thirteen thousand BCE is seven thousand years before the Areni men and about twelve thousand years before anybody wrote anything down. **This archive already made this argument** once, at length, about the ancient-genome scores further up this page, and the conclusion is the same one: a shared ancestor in the Palaeolithic is a fact about the species, not about a household. The feature itself calls these **«fun facts»**, which is the most honest label on the whole screen.

It is recorded here so that nobody has to go looking for it twice.

next.heading: What would actually settle it
rows: **This is the whole answer, and it is cheap.** Any male-line descendant of the surname — from Senj, Pićan, Vodnjan, Gračišće, Mione, anywhere — taking a Y test would say in one stroke whether **L-M27 belongs to the surname** or **entered this particular branch of it**. Two men who share a documented male-line ancestor and share a haplogroup close the question. Two who share the ancestor and not the haplogroup locate the break between them.

Sequences the chromosome properly instead of sampling it. It would confirm or overturn the chip call, place the line on a dated branch, and return a list of men who share it — which is the only route to a **surname** rather than a continent.

Nothing on this page removes a single documented link. Every father-and-son pair in this archive was put there by a clerk who watched it happen, and a haplogroup does not unwrite a baptism. What the Y does is ask a question **above** the paper — in the century the registers do not reach.

ydna.ydnasource: MyHeritage DNA → Y-DNA, powered by **FamilyTreeDNA**, read 14 September 2026 from David's own account: David's kit and the kit of his father, both returning **L-M27**. Country frequencies, ancient connections and notable connections as displayed on that date. Ancient samples I1634 and I1632 are from **Lazaridis et al. 2016**; the Sayyid Ajall study is **Chuan-Chao Wang et al.**, *Present Y chromosomes support the Persian ancestry of Sayyid Ajall Shams al-Din Omar and Eminent Navigator Zheng He*. The **Time Tree was not read** — it is behind the Big Y-700 upgrade.
